messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 55
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: North American
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Fashion Designer
  trauma_type: Physical abuse by caregiver (childhood)
  pcl5: 41

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Other-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what other people have done to me, Avoid Dreams: Situations or times of day that tend to bring on nightmares, Self-Blame Rumination: I dwell on what I have done wrong
  Threat: Startle to Touch: I react with alarm when someone touches me unexpectedly, Threat in Silence: Unusual silence makes me feel something dangerous is about to happen, Alert at Home: I feel on guard even inside my own home
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, Emotionless Recall: Sometimes I can recall what happened but feel completely numb, as if it happened to a stranger, Guilt on Recall: When I remember the event I feel intense guilt
  Negative Appraisals: Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse, Mistrust: People can't be trusted, Fear Going Crazy: My reactions since the event mean that I am going crazy

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Threat
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Memory → Threat
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Threat → Memory
  - Threat → Negative Appraisals
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Memory
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Negative Appraisals

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Arthur presents as a man immaculately assembled, his bespoke suits and measured speech conveying a lifetime of success in the demanding world of fashion design. At 55, he is at the pinnacle of his career, yet he speaks of a profound and accelerating collapse. The trauma is not recent; it is the bedrock of his life, laid down in the terrifying quiet of his childhood home. He speaks of his stepfather, a man whose presence was preceded by an unnerving silence that would settle over the house. This silence was the real threat, the indicator that violence was imminent. Decades later, it is still the silence that undoes him. An unexpected lull in the bustling energy of his design studio can trigger a cascade of physiological fear, a certainty that something dangerous is about to happen.

The memories of that time do not exist for him as a coherent story. Instead, they are a collection of sensory fragments and disjointed scenes he cannot sequence. Often, when a piece of the past surfaces, it is with a chilling numbness; he recalls an image of himself as a small boy, hiding, but feels nothing, as if watching a stranger in a film. This emotional distance is a fragile defence. A sudden jolt of threat—the unnerving quiet, or an assistant placing an unexpected hand on his shoulder in the studio—can shatter it, bringing forth not a narrative but a raw, fragmented image of his stepfather’s face or the pattern of the wallpaper in the hall. This sudden intrusion of the past confirms his feeling of being constantly on guard, even in his own locked apartment, and the heightened sense of threat, in turn, makes the memories feel more present and powerful, ready to ambush him at any moment.

When the memories do carry an emotional charge, it is almost always one of intense, suffocating guilt. He is haunted by the question of his own inaction, the passivity of the child he was. This guilt has become the lens through which he views himself, cementing a powerful conviction that he is permanently damaged. The memories serve as relentless proof for his deepest beliefs: that he has been changed for the worse by what happened, and that his volatile reactions now—the startling at a touch, the panic in the silence—are evidence that he is, in his own words, "going crazy." This deep mistrust in his own mind has bled outwards, fostering a pervasive belief that other people, at their core, cannot be trusted.

These deeply held negative appraisals dictate the landscape of his daily life. The core belief that people are untrustworthy means he exists in a constant state of low-grade alert, scanning for betrayal or harm. This hypervigilance also shapes his memory; the conviction that he is irreparably broken makes it impossible for him to construct a story of survival, leaving only a catalogue of shame and damage. In an effort to manage these overwhelming feelings, Arthur has, over decades, fallen into punishing cognitive routines. His belief that he is damaged and others are dangerous fuels hours of rumination. He spends long nights dwelling on his stepfather’s cruelty, replaying every injustice. But just as often, the blame turns inward, and he exhaustively catalogues his own perceived failures, dissecting what he should have done differently as a helpless child.

These ruminative cycles do not bring clarity or relief; they are the engine of his distress. They prevent the memories from ever being filed away as past events, instead dragging the fragmented images back into the present, each loop of self-blame or anger re-sensitising him to the original trauma. Furthermore, this constant mental churn only serves to strengthen his most painful conclusions about himself. The more he dwells on what was done to him and what he failed to do, the more convinced he becomes that he is fundamentally broken and that his inability to simply "get over it" is a sign of irreversible personal failure. He has tried to manage the consequences, meticulously avoiding situations that might lead to nightmares, often working late into the night until he is too exhausted to dream. This has taken a toll on his relationships, contributing to his divorce two years ago. His ex-wife described him as living behind a wall of glass, present but unreachable. It is this encroaching isolation, and a terrifying sense that his creative focus is finally beginning to fracture under the strain, that has brought him to therapy. He is afraid he is losing the one part of his life he felt he could control, and he is desperate for proof that he is not, in fact, going crazy.
